assertion.name: Vertical transmission
assertion.description: Maternal varicella infection during pregnancy can result in transplacental transmission to the fetus. assertion.name: Direct contact with vesicle fluid
assertion.description: Transmission also occurs through direct contact with fluid from vesicular lesions. Vesicle fluid contains high titers of infectious VZV. This route is particularly important in household and healthcare settings where close physical contact occurs.

selected_evidence.snippet: Infection with varicella zoster virus (VZV) causes varicella (chickenpox), which can be severe in immunocompromised individuals, infants and adults.

assertion.name: Airborne/respiratory droplet transmission
assertion.description: VZV is transmitted primarily via the airborne route through inhalation of infectious aerosols or respiratory droplets from an infected individual. The virus is well-recognized as an airborne pathogen alongside measles and tuberculosis, requiring airborne infection isolation precautions (N95 respirators) in healthcare settings. The infectious period extends from 1-2 days before rash onset until all lesions have crusted over.

selected_evidence.snippet: Chickenpox is an extremely contagious infectious disease caused by varicella zoster virus (VZV).

assertion.name: Endogenous haematogenous seeding during bacteraemia or fungaemia
assertion.description: The minority route. Organisms circulating in the blood cross the blood-retinal barrier and seed the eye, so the eye is a metastatic site of a systemic infection rather than the point of entry. Pathogens reach the highly vascular choroid first and spread into the vitreous from there, which is why these cases are often bilateral and present against a background of systemic illness such as endocarditis, liver abscess, indwelling catheters, or candidaemia. Spread runs one way only: an infected eye is never itself a source of bacteraemia.

selected_evidence.snippet: The infected eye never serves as a source of bacteraemia or fungaemia, however.

assertion.name: Exogenous inoculation through a breach of the globe
assertion.description: The common route. Organisms are introduced directly into the eye when the globe is opened, by intraocular surgery, penetrating trauma, intravitreal injection, a filtering bleb, or extension from an infected cornea. The inoculum is usually the patient's own periocular and conjunctival flora at the moment the barrier is breached, which is why the organism recovered tracks the route of entry rather than any systemic source.

selected_evidence.snippet: This breach may occur following intraocular surgery, penetrating trauma, or intravitreal injections.

assertion.name: Exogenous inoculation through a breach of the globe
assertion.description: The common route. Organisms are introduced directly into the eye when the globe is opened, by intraocular surgery, penetrating trauma, intravitreal injection, a filtering bleb, or extension from an infected cornea. The inoculum is usually the patient's own periocular and conjunctival flora at the moment the barrier is breached, which is why the organism recovered tracks the route of entry rather than any systemic source.

selected_evidence.snippet: Most cases are exogenous and occur after eye surgery, after penetrating ocular trauma, or as an extension of corneal infection.

selected_evidence.snippet: Exogenous endophthalmitis, the more common subtype, results from direct inoculation of microorganisms into the eye.

assertion.name: Endogenous haematogenous seeding during bacteraemia or fungaemia
assertion.description: The minority route. Organisms circulating in the blood cross the blood-retinal barrier and seed the eye, so the eye is a metastatic site of a systemic infection rather than the point of entry. Pathogens reach the highly vascular choroid first and spread into the vitreous from there, which is why these cases are often bilateral and present against a background of systemic illness such as endocarditis, liver abscess, indwelling catheters, or candidaemia. Spread runs one way only: an infected eye is never itself a source of bacteraemia.

selected_evidence.snippet: Endophthalmitis may also be endogenous, arising from bacteraemic or fungaemic seeding of the eye.
